section_summary: This section closes a 1936 Navy report alleging espionage and other unlawful activity by Japanese naval vessels and residents in Hawaii, then documents the 1937 interdepartmental effort to formulate a federal response. The papers review suspicious tanker visits, possible clandestine landing of naval personnel, military photography, propaganda, and the use of Japanese-operated fishing vessels for observation or covert movement. Proposed remedies included surveillance at Honolulu, restrictions on visits to other Hawaiian ports, stricter customs and immigration enforcement, identification of fishing crews, diplomatic representations to Japan, and new federal and territorial legislation.

subfiles.title: Concluding findings on Japanese naval and civilian activities in Hawaii
subfiles.to: Secretary of the Navy and other federal officials
subfiles.about: Concludes that Japanese ship visits and associated local activity may violate espionage, customs, and territorial laws and recommends investigation and executive action.
subfiles.summary: The concluding paragraphs characterize the Tsurumi's reconnaissance of Midway and the Ondo crew's photography, measurements, sketches, and customs violations at Hilo and Waimea as inimical to American defense. They recommend further State Department investigation, possible representations to Japan, and direction from the President to Hawaiian and federal authorities. The report finds existing statutes generally sufficient if officials obtain proof and are willing to act; Claude A. Swanson approved it on September 18, 1936.

subfiles.title: Department of State routing note on confidential material
subfiles.from: Department of State, Office of Coordination and Review
subfiles.about: Records confidential handling and contemplated hand delivery of material to the War Department.
subfiles.summary: The fragmentary note appears to record that an item was placed under double cover for the War Department. It also indicates intended delivery by hand on the following morning.

subfiles.title: Designation of Stanley K. Hornbeck for preliminary discussions
subfiles.about: Names Stanley K. Hornbeck as the State Department representative in preliminary discussions of Japanese activities in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Woodring's request for interdepartmental study of objectionable activities by visiting and resident Japanese in Hawaii. He designates Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, and assumes that Woodring will summon the departmental representatives.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting California Joint Immigration Committee Document No. 501
subfiles.from: California Joint Immigration Committee; V. S. McClatchy
subfiles.about: Supplies a document omitted from a footnote in the committee's June 18 statement.
subfiles.summary: The California Joint Immigration Committee advises Hull that its June 18 statement omitted a reference to Document No. 501. A copy of that document, concerning alleged Japanese propaganda in public schools, is enclosed.

subfiles.title: More Japanese Propaganda in the Public Schools
subfiles.about: Accuses the American Council of the Institute of Pacific Relations and associated textbook writers of presenting misleading pro-Japanese material in schools.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews disputed textbooks introduced in Hawaiian and California schools and notes that earlier books were withdrawn or corrected after protests. It singles out Helen Pratt's Japan, Where Ancient Loyalties Survive for allegedly obscuring facts about the Gentlemen's Agreement, exclusion, immigration, and Japanese policy in Asia. The committee argues that the treatment deliberately misleads students and instructors in Japan's favor.

subfiles.title: Internal note requesting Wilson's attendance
subfiles.about: Reports that the Secretary wants Hugh R. Wilson to attend the committee meeting and receive background on the case.
subfiles.summary: The note says Mr. Renchard called concerning the case. It conveys the Secretary's instruction that Wilson attend the meeting and asks Hamilton to brief him on the background.

subfiles.title: State Department concerns about proposed fisheries legislation
subfiles.about: Explains two provisions in the draft committee report and cautions against legislation that would broadly eliminate alien ownership of fishing vessels.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that one proposed measure would identify alien fishermen through devices such as fingerprints, while another would amend Revised Statutes section 4311 to make fishing vessels eventually citizen-owned. The Department believes espionage-related abuses can be controlled without a measure that might violate commercial treaties, deprive resident aliens of their livelihoods, and provoke retaliation against Americans abroad.

subfiles.title: Invitation to consider the Working Committee report
subfiles.about: Invites the Secretary of State to a November 17 meeting of the Interdepartmental Committee to consider the Working Committee's completed report.
subfiles.summary: Woodring recalls the President's creation of the committee on Japanese naval and civil activity in Hawaii and the Interior Department's subsequent participation. He reports that the Working Committee has finished its work, encloses its report and proposed letter to the President, and proposes a meeting in his office.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Secretary of War on Japanese activities in Hawaii
subfiles.about: Summarizes the committee's origin, membership, assigned problem, and principal concerns before transmitting recommendations.
subfiles.summary: Krueger recounts the October 1936 War and Navy warning, the President's May 1937 direction to form an interdepartmental committee, and the addition of the Interior Department. He lists the departmental representatives and identifies the practices under review: clandestine landing of Japanese personnel, unauthorized military presence, suspicious craft, special photography, and the landing of observation equipment. A draft letter to the President contains the committee's conclusions and recommendations.

subfiles.title: Draft letter to the President recommending measures against Japanese activities in Hawaii
subfiles.from: Secretary of War as chairman of the Interdepartmental Committee
subfiles.about: Recommends administrative controls and legislation to counter suspected Japanese espionage and covert activity in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The draft proposes limiting Japanese public vessels to Honolulu, covertly counting persons leaving and boarding them, strengthening customs observation, regulating alien-operated fishing boats, and making representations to Japan after violations. It also urges priority for S. 1485, restricting photography of defense installations, and an amendment to R.S. 4311 that would ultimately require fishing vessels to be citizen-owned. The measures address clandestine personnel landings, suspicious craft, photography, and specialized observation equipment.

subfiles.title: Designation of Wilson and Hamilton for the November 17 meeting
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the committee meeting and designates Hugh R. Wilson and Maxwell M. Hamilton to represent the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Hull confirms receipt of Woodring's November 10 invitation to consider the Working Committee report. He appoints Assistant Secretary Hugh R. Wilson as his representative, accompanied by Maxwell M. Hamilton of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs.

subfiles.title: Record of the November 17 Interdepartmental Committee meeting
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs files
subfiles.about: Records approval of the draft presidential letter with a State Department qualification concerning foreign relations.
subfiles.summary: The committee met in the Secretary of War's office with Woodring presiding. It approved the draft letter to the President after adding the words “having due regard for our foreign relations” to the legislative recommendation, a change proposed by the State Department representatives.

subfiles.title: Attendance list for the November 17 Interdepartmental Committee meeting
subfiles.about: Lists the departmental representatives expected at the meeting on Japanese naval and civil personnel in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The statement names Wilson and Hamilton for State, Waesche for Treasury, Ingersoll for Navy, Slattery for Interior, and Houghteling and Wixon for Labor. It notes that the Attorney General would send no representative but assented by letter to transmitting the proposed report to the President.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Guy M. Gillette letter on Japanese consular activities
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a Gillette letter concerning alleged Japanese consular organization of Asian residents against Caucasian citizens in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference identifies a November 26, 1937 letter from Guy M. Gillette filed elsewhere. It says the letter reports evidence developed by the commission investigating Hawaiian statehood about allegedly improper Japanese consular activity.

subfiles.title: Notification of presidential approval of the committee report
subfiles.about: Reports that the President approved the committee report and ordered its recommendations implemented quickly.
subfiles.summary: Woodring states that the President fully approved the November 17 report and directed him to notify the committee members to put the recommendations into effect. The President also requested confidential letters to the appropriate House and Senate chairmen regarding the proposed legislation, and those drafts had been submitted for signature.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of presidential approval
subfiles.about: Acknowledges notice that the President approved the committee report and requested prompt implementation and congressional action.
subfiles.summary: Hull records Woodring's notice that the President approved the November 17 report and wanted its measures executed as quickly as possible. He also notes that Woodring prepared letters for the relevant congressional chairmen about the committee's legislative proposals.

subfiles.title: Supplementary Report: Activities of Japanese Naval and Civil Personnel in Hawaii
subfiles.from: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, and Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Presents additional naval intelligence about suspicious Japanese tanker visits to Honolulu and an incident involving a U.S. sailor.
subfiles.summary: The report reviews visits by the Tsurumi, Sata, Ondo, Rimo, and Hayatomo, alleging that the ships maintained contacts, spread propaganda, carried unlisted persons, and left officers or enlisted men in Honolulu. It suggests that these visits created a communication channel and an organization capable of observing forthcoming U.S. Army and Navy exercises. It also describes the forcible removal of sailor Arthur J. Carroll to a police station after he photographed the Japanese Consul-General on a Navy pier.

subfiles.title: War and Navy concerns requiring action in Hawaii
subfiles.about: Defines the Japanese naval and civilian practices that the War and Navy Departments particularly wanted terminated.
subfiles.summary: Krueger identifies suspected landing of naval and military personnel, unauthorized Japanese service members, suspicious craft, and photography of ships, Pearl Harbor, and defense installations. He also cites special cameras, range finders, and surveying instruments landed from ships, including incidents reported by Mrs. Kanakanui at Hilo and sailors photographing fortifications from the Royal Hawaiian Hotel.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Irving F. Wixon's immigration memorandum
subfiles.about: Forwards Wixon's secret analysis of immigration issues affecting Japanese naval and civilian personnel in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Krueger circulates a memorandum prepared by Labor Department representative Irving F. Wixon. The enclosure is supplied for the Working Committee's information and consideration during its study.

subfiles.title: Immigration and Naturalization Service analysis of Japanese personnel and fishing vessels
subfiles.about: Explains legal and practical obstacles to identifying and deporting Japanese personnel and checking crews of Hawaiian fishing vessels.
subfiles.summary: Wixon reports Coast Guard-assisted inspections of Japanese fishing sampans, including arrests and the voluntary departure of suspected stowaways or deserters. He argues that crews should carry photographic, fingerprinted identification because the boats follow no fixed schedule and their crews can change at sea. The memorandum also explains the evidentiary and limitation problems in deportation cases and warns that singling out Japanese naval vessels for immigration examination could create diplomatic embarrassment.

subfiles.title: Call for another Working Committee meeting
subfiles.about: Proposes a September 21 meeting to formulate constructive recommendations on Japanese activities in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Krueger reviews the earlier committee meeting, his July 2 statement of War and Navy concerns, and Wixon's subsequent immigration analysis. He suggests that the Working Committee reconvene at the Winder Building to prepare recommendations for the full Interdepartmental Committee.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck response to the proposed September 21 meeting
subfiles.about: Confirms that Hornbeck has reserved the proposed meeting date and will attend or send a substitute.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck acknowledges Krueger's August 31 memorandum proposing a September 21 Working Committee meeting. He places the date on his calendar and indicates that either he or a substitute will attend.

subfiles.title: Foreign public vessel notices and possible misinterpretation
subfiles.about: Questions whether standard courtesy notices for foreign public vessels might be misread as granting customs or immigration immunity.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Buford explains that the notices are intended only to inform other departments and not to exempt foreign-vessel personnel from customs or immigration rules. The memorandum suggests adopting more explicit wording because Treasury and Labor field officers may misinterpret the existing form.

subfiles.title: Handwritten note concerning checks of foreign public vessels
subfiles.about: Contains fragmentary comments concerning whether Labor or Customs authorities should check a foreign vessel and refers to an attachment.
subfiles.summary: The handwriting is largely illegible because of poor OCR. The readable portions appear to discuss checking a vessel through Labor or Customs and direct attention to an attached form.

subfiles.title: Standard Department of State request for courtesies to a public vessel
subfiles.about: Provides standard language requesting the usual courtesies and facilities when no objection is perceived.
subfiles.summary: The form presents the Secretary of State's compliments and requests customary courtesies in a specified case. Its incomplete recipient and case fields show that it served as the specimen wording discussed in the preceding memorandum.

subfiles.title: Hamilton review of subcommittee recommendations
subfiles.about: Seeks approval to accept Ingersoll's draft recommendations for presentation to the full committee.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton explains that he, Ingersoll, and Wixon were appointed to a subcommittee on Japanese naval and civil activity in Hawaii. He considers Ingersoll's recommendations generally satisfactory, though he flags the new proposal to bar Japanese public vessels from Hawaiian ports other than Honolulu. Hamilton recommends raising no objection at that stage.

subfiles.title: State Department note on reciprocal restrictions on naval port visits
subfiles.about: Considers the legal and diplomatic implications of excluding Japanese vessels from Hawaiian ports.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum finds no reason to distinguish Japan's refusal of American naval visits to mandated-island ports from an American right to refuse Japanese visits to Hawaii. It nevertheless questions whether retaliation is timely because U.S. naval vessels had begun visiting Kobe without difficulty and restrictions might provoke Japanese obstruction or other diplomatic friction.

subfiles.title: Ingersoll letter transmitting draft subcommittee recommendations
subfiles.about: Forwards suggested recommendations on the matters referred to the Hawaii subcommittee.
subfiles.summary: Ingersoll sends Hamilton a proposed draft for the subcommittee's recommendations. He notes that Irving F. Wixon is receiving a copy as the third subcommittee member.

subfiles.title: Recommendations for surveillance of Japanese naval vessels
subfiles.from: Subcommittee of Ingersoll, Hamilton, and Wixon
subfiles.about: Proposes covert counts, customs surveillance, diplomatic reporting, and limits on Japanese public-vessel visits in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The recommendations call for independent, concealed counts of uniformed officers, enlisted men, and civilians leaving or boarding Japanese vessels at Honolulu under Fourteenth Naval District supervision. Any discrepancy would be reported to State for representations or other action. They also recommend denying visits to other Hawaiian ports and covert customs observation for illicit landings of material.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of proposed Working Committee report
subfiles.about: Circulates a proposed report and calls a November 5 meeting to consider it.
subfiles.summary: Krueger submits a draft report intended for the chairman of the Interdepartmental Committee. He proposes that the Working Committee meet at the Winder Building on November 5 to review the text.

subfiles.title: Draft Working Committee report for the Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Sets out the committee's mandate, membership, concerns, and submission of a draft presidential letter.
subfiles.summary: The report recounts the formation of the interdepartmental body and the addition of the Interior Department. It lists the representatives and the five principal concerns involving covertly landed personnel, unauthorized service members, suspicious craft, military photography, and specialized observation equipment. It transmits the committee's recommendations in a draft letter to the President.

subfiles.title: Golden W. Bell's proposed revisions to the committee report
subfiles.about: Suggests revisions referring to accompanying legislative materials and describing the proposed measures as supplements to existing controls.
subfiles.summary: Bell proposes that the report expressly transmit copies of congressional bills and proposed Hawaiian legislation along with the draft letter. He also suggests stating that the new measures would supplement existing ones. His proposed fisheries paragraph would have the Interior Department sponsor a Hawaiian bill similar to S. 1485 and other committee legislation to regulate alien-operated boats and crews.

subfiles.title: Revised draft letter to the President on Japanese activities in Hawaii
subfiles.from: Secretary of War as chairman of the Interdepartmental Committee
subfiles.about: Presents the committee's revised administrative and legislative recommendations.
subfiles.summary: The revised draft recommends restricting Japanese public vessels to Honolulu, covertly checking personnel, watching for customs violations, regulating alien-operated fishing boats, and making representations to Japan. It further urges high priority for S. 1485 and an amendment to R.S. 4311 that would eventually require citizen ownership of fishing vessels. The letter frames these measures as supplements to existing controls against espionage and covert military observation.

subfiles.title: Earlier draft memorandum for the Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Provides another draft account of the committee's creation, membership, concerns, and recommendation process.
subfiles.summary: This draft repeats the history of the October 1936 warning and the President's May 1937 establishment of the interdepartmental body. It identifies the departmental representatives and the practices the War and Navy Departments wanted stopped in Hawaii. The Working Committee reports that its conclusions are embodied in an attached draft letter to the President.

subfiles.title: Earlier draft letter to the President
subfiles.from: Secretary of War as chairman of the Interdepartmental Committee
subfiles.about: Recommends port, surveillance, customs, diplomatic, and legislative measures, with a notation that part had not yet received State Department approval.
subfiles.summary: The draft proposes excluding Japanese public vessels from Hawaiian ports other than Honolulu, counting their personnel, intensifying customs scrutiny, regulating alien-operated fishing boats, and acting after definite violations. It advocates S. 1485 and an amendment to R.S. 4311 that would ultimately displace alien ownership of fishing vessels. A marginal notation states that the vessel-ownership provision had not yet been approved by the State Department.

subfiles.title: Cover sheet for papers supplied by Captain Munter
subfiles.about: Identifies the following material as a copy of papers furnished by Captain Munter.
subfiles.summary: The page is a brief cover notation rather than a substantive memorandum. It attributes the accompanying papers to Captain Munter, acting for the Treasury Department's Coast Guard representative.

subfiles.title: Excerpt from Commander Towle's letter on Japanese fishing vessels
subfiles.about: Reports discussions with Mr. Bland and military officers about controlling Japanese-owned fishing vessels and crews in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Towle describes Hawaii's fishing industry as largely controlled by Japanese owners and crews and recounts a conference with Bland, Naval Intelligence, Navy, and Army officers about proposed federal legislation. He argues that alien-owned small craft concentrated at Hawaii, San Pedro, and San Diego pose a strategic danger and urges identification papers, Coast Guard enforcement authority, and controls on vessel ownership and operation. He also proposes amendments to Hawaiian statutes governing fishermen's tags, vessel-registration data, citizenship declarations, and penalties, while noting political resistance to broad alien-registration measures.

subfiles.title: Commander Towle's proposed amendment to the federal vessel-numbering law
subfiles.to: U.S. Coast Guard and congressional reviewers
subfiles.about: Would impose citizenship, ownership, identification, permitting, and national-defense conditions on numbered vessels.
subfiles.summary: The proposal requires detailed vessel data and an owner's oath that no foreign subject has an interest in the craft and that it will not prejudice national defense. Aliens aboard numbered vessels would need federal identification certificates, while operators would have to be citizens, speak English, and obtain permits for trade or fishing. Violations would expose owners, operators, and vessels to fines, forfeiture, or seizure.

subfiles.title: Proposed amendment to Revised Statutes section 4311
subfiles.to: W. Y. Towle; information copy for R. R. Waesche
subfiles.about: Proposes restricting the coasting trade and fisheries to licensed American vessels while allowing a temporary exception for certain resident-alien owners.
subfiles.summary: The amendment defines which licensed vessels may engage in the coasting trade or fisheries and subjects unauthorized vessels to forfeiture. It exempts very small citizen-owned craft and grants lawfully resident alien owners a six-year transition for fishing vessels. The notation says Bland gave the secret proposal to Towle for study and comment and that it was for Admiral Waesche's information only.

subfiles.title: S. 1485: Bill to prohibit photographs, sketches, or maps of vital defense installations
subfiles.from: David I. Walsh and Morris Sheppard
subfiles.to: United States Senate Committee on Naval Affairs
subfiles.about: Would criminalize unauthorized recording and dissemination of designated military and naval installations and equipment.
subfiles.summary: S. 1485 authorizes the President to designate vital military and naval installations or equipment requiring protection and requires command permission and censorship for photographs, sketches, maps, and similar representations. It applies the same penalty to the use of aircraft for unauthorized recording and restricts reproduction or publication of uncensored material. The bill extends to U.S. territories, possessions, the high seas, naval vessels, aircraft, and separate military or naval commands, with penalties of up to $1,000, one year in prison, or both.
